newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish parliament passes money laundering law.
newsitem.headline: Turkish parliament passes money laundering law.

text.p: Turkey's parliament has passed a law aimed at curbing money laundering as part of the country's fight against organised crime, particularly drug smuggling.
Turkey is a major transit point for heroin moving from Asia to western Europe and the passage of the law has been seen by politicians as a step towards combating the trade.
The law, passed unanimously by deputies late on Wednesday, envisages the creation of an authority to investigate financial crimes which will pass on its findings to public prosecutors.
Speaking ahead of the vote, deputy Biltekin Ozdemir told parliament that some public employees and politicians were mixed up in organised crime.

"Money laundering is dirtying the state and state employees. Shady activities are increasing. These regulations will help to clean up politics and the administration," said Ozdemir from the opposition Motherland Party.
Speculation about links between the Turkish state and mafia has been rife since a police official and a wanted gangster were killed in the same car.

Former interior minister Mehmet Agar resigned after the crash, which has now become the subject of court and parliament investigations. A Kurdish warlord, Sedat Bucak, who serves as a government MP, was injured in the crash.

Under the new law, authorities will be able to seize possessions or freeze accounts believed to be connected with money laundering. A two to five year sentence will be imposed on anyone found to be involved in money laundering.
The law aims to counter arms smuggling, blackmail, kidnapping and other organised crime activities by restricting the ability of criminals to use the country's financial system.

A minimum four year sentence will be imposed for money laundering which is found to be linked to guerrilla activities. Deputies pointed to the separatist Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) as being heavily involved in drug trafficking.
True Path Party deputy Sait Acba said 40 percent of drugs trade in Turkey was controlled by the PKK, which is fighting for self-rule in southeast Turkey.
Turkish security forces seized 3.4 tonnes of heroin in 1995, more than a fifth of all the heroin seized worldwide.
